title: Dustin Poirier Reveals Bud Light Terminated His Contract Immediately After Airport Arrest
excerpt: The retired UFC star confirmed that Bud Light ended their sponsorship deal right after his public drunkenness arrest in Atlanta, saying he doesn't need 'that poison' in his life anymore.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Dustin Poirier's contract with Bud Light ended immediately after his June 21 arrest for public drunkenness.
  • The sponsorship, worth six figures, began in March 2024 and included prominent advertising campaigns.
  • Poirier's airport incident was triggered by personal issues related to his father's alcoholism and homelessness.
  • UFC champion Sean Strickland criticized Bud Light's decision, calling it un-American and hypocritical.
  • Poirier remains committed to sobriety and is exploring future opportunities in broadcasting and boxing.
https://x.com/MMAFighting/status/2079674183613817269

From Brand Partner to Dropped Sponsor

Dustin Poirier has now confirmed what many in the MMA world had suspected: Bud Light ended their sponsorship deal with him immediately after his arrest for public drunkenness last month.

Speaking during the UFC Oklahoma City broadcast on July 21, the 37-year-old retired fighter revealed that Bud Light "terminated my contract immediately" following the June 21 incident at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, where he was arrested after confronting airport employees and a police officer while intoxicated.

The sponsorship, which Poirier secured in March 2024, was reportedly worth six figures. He had been featured prominently in multiple Bud Light campaigns alongside UFC announcer Bruce Buffer, including a widely aired "Call Center" commercial that ran during UFC broadcasts throughout 2025 and early 2026.

The Airport Incident That Changed Everything

Poirier's troubles began on Father's Day, June 21, 2026, when he was arrested at the Atlanta airport after being denied boarding on a Delta flight. Body camera footage released by the Atlanta Police Department showed the former interim UFC lightweight champion behaving aggressively, threatening to fight a police officer, and using a racial slur.

Broader Fallout and Financial Impact

The Bud Light termination was just one piece of the financial fallout. Poirier previously revealed that the arrest cost him "a lot of money," including three scheduled gigs that week and at least one other major sponsor. He also expressed uncertainty about the future of his broadcasting career with Paramount+, where he had been working as a UFC desk analyst since his retirement.

"They terminated my contract immediately. But I don't need that f***ing poison in my life."

— Dustin Poirier, during UFC Oklahoma City broadcast

"Obviously, the gigs, the three things I was supposed to do that week are gone. And then a big sponsor of mine is gone because of it," Poirier said during an earlier appearance. "I'm losing gigs and losing things that I had set up."

Bud Light had been the official beer partner of the UFC since January 2024 under a multiyear deal with Anheuser-Busch. Poirier was absent from the brand's commercial that aired during UFC 329 on July 12, which featured only Bruce Buffer — a notable departure from previous ads that included both men.

Strickland's Defense and the MMA Community's Response

UFC middleweight champion Sean Strickland, who initially mocked Poirier's struggles with mental health, reversed course after speaking privately with the retired fighter. Strickland then directed pointed criticism at Bud Light in an Instagram video that went viral in the MMA community.

Strickland also shared that his own father's alcoholism had shaped his initial harsh reaction, admitting his upbringing "turned him into a monster" and that alcohol abuse triggers deep childhood trauma for him.

A Pattern in Combat Sports Sponsorships

Poirier's situation echoes a familiar pattern in combat sports. Conor McGregor lost sponsorships with Proximo Spirits and game studio IO Interactive after assault allegations. Former heavyweight champion Jon Jones was dropped by Nike and Reebok following separate off-cage incidents, including the 2015 Albuquerque hit-and-run case.

"You spent $6 billion creating an addict."**

"I'll fight you right now," Poirier told the officer in the footage. "Let's go. Yeah, tell 'em. Tell 'em to come on, because it's going to be bad."

He was booked into Clayton County Jail at 6:38 p.m. and released later that evening. In Georgia, public drunkenness is a misdemeanor that carries up to a year in jail and a $1,000 fine.

Poirier later explained in a candid interview on "The Diary of a CEO" podcast that his father's ongoing struggles with alcoholism and homelessness had triggered the episode.

"He's actually homeless right now. Part of that, me getting drunk at the airport — and it's not my weight to carry — but I tried to help him, and he's back on the street. On Father's Day, I was traveling to work and I just couldn't stop thinking about my father."

— Dustin Poirier, on The Diary of a CEO podcast

However, critics argue that an alcohol brand terminating a partnership because an athlete struggled with alcohol represents a different kind of hypocrisy — a point Strickland drove home by highlighting Anheuser-Busch's revenue.

What Lies Ahead for Poirier

Despite the setbacks, Poirier has committed to sobriety and says his family — wife Jolie and their two children — "deserve me at 100 percent." He continues to appear on UFC broadcasts and has not ruled out a return to fighting, putting the chances at "five percent." He remains under contract with the UFC and has expressed interest in a potential boxing career, though UFC contractual obligations currently prevent that.

Chance of returning to fighting

Poirier, who retired with a 30-10 professional record after a unanimous decision loss to Max Holloway at UFC 318 in July 2025, built his legacy on signature victories over Conor McGregor (twice), Justin Gaethje, Eddie Alvarez, and Max Holloway. He also co-founded The Good Fight Foundation with his wife in 2018, a charitable organization supporting families in his home state of Louisiana.

As he navigates this turbulent chapter, Poirier's willingness to speak publicly about his struggles has earned widespread support from the MMA community — even from former critics like Strickland. Whether that goodwill translates into new sponsorship opportunities remains to be seen.

The broader conversation about alcohol brands profiting from consumption while distancing themselves from addiction resonates globally.
